0.title: Collaborate
0.content: The heart of our mission is collaboration We bring people together for events like Douglass Day, an international celebration of Black history and activism occurring yearly on or near February 14, the date that Frederick Douglass chose to celebrate as his birthday. Geneseo students, faculty, and staff join a live stream hosted by the Douglass Day organizers at the Center for Black Digital Research at Penn State and elsewhere, and they participate in collaborative transcription of digitized documents important to Black history and culture. See our local Douglass Day site for photos, videos, and other documentation of our yearly participation in this event. We’ve also brought people together for Ada Lovelace Day, a yearly international celebration of women in STEM that we’ve also treated locally as a celebration of connections between the natural sciences and the arts and humanities. Ada Lovelace, the nineteenth-century mathematician widely regarded as a pioneer in the thinking that led to the development of digital computing, was the daughter of British romantic poet George Gordon, Lord Byron. The CDL’s own work is highly collaborative. To help advance digital learning, pedagogy, and scholarship, we work together with instructional designers and programmers in the department of Computing and Information Technology (CIT) and with our colleagues in Milne Library, the Teaching and Learning Center, the Center for Integrative Learning, the Office of Accessibility Services, the Office of Multicultural Affairs, and the Career Design Center. The CDL contributes to and occasionally leads efforts to develop institutional guidance with respect to campus technology, whether in areas like online learning or artificial intelligence. The CDL director is a member of Geneseo’s newly formed workforce development team, which advances the college’s equity-centered liberal arts mission through career education and community partnerships.

1.title: Create
1.content: Let us help you build Whether you’re looking to share research or creative projects with a wide audience, publicize your campus office’s services to potential users, complete a digital project for a class, or just establish a digital presence with an online portfolio, we can help you get a website up and running to accomplish the task. Because our goal is to empower, we won’t design, build, or maintain the site for you, but we’ll help you choose the right tools to realize your vision and provide support as you do the work. Anyone with a Geneseo account can create a personal or collaborative WordPress site on Geneseo OpenLab. If your project requires a different kind of site — say an Omeka site for building exhibits with digitized archival materials, or a Wikipedia-like site for building a collaborative knowledge resource — we can help you set up shared hosting on SUNY Create. There are other options for building and hosting sites: static-site generators like Jekyll or Zola, free hosting from GitHub or other providers, and commercial hosting plans. We can help you with open-source tools to enhance your website. TimelineJS and StoryMapJS are just two of many. If you need help with a tool we don’t know about or have limited experience with, ask us about it! We’ll look into it. We’re always eager to expand our own toolkit.

2.title: Explore
2.content: Use our resources – and help us improve them In addition to working directly with students, faculty, and staff — individually or in groups — the CDL advances digital learning and scholarship on campus through online resources, many of which you’ll find referenced elsewhere on this website. Examples include Creative Commons-licensed educational resources that anyone can use for their own learning or adapt for teaching others, such as Crtical Digital Practices and Life in Plain Text. The virtual commons Geneseo OpenLab, where any member of the Geneseo community can launch a personal or collaborative website. Take a look at how the Center for Integrative Learning is using OpenLab to showcase how Geneseo students are meeting the college’s integrative and applied learning requirement through interdisciplinary coursework, study abroad, and guided research; or at how students working with Professors Michael Oberg and Alla Myzelev used it to build Chenussio, a website exploring the indigenous history of Livingston County; or at how students and faculty in Music have used it to create a companion website to a live gallery exhibition of event posters from Geneseo’s past in Dorm Rooms Through the Decades; or at how students like Laura Wright (’25) and Gwenyth Harrington (’27) have used it to build sites for their individual research projects. (The CDL helped Wright and Harrington spin off their OpenLab sites to free-standing ones on domains they own themselves: Educational Equity Watch and Transcribing Verse, respectively.) The community-sourced information and opinion forum GenAI: Generative AI at Geneseo, a moderated OpenLab site where any member of the Geneseo community can contribute content related to the uses and impact of AI, with special attention to how it’s affecting teaching and learning on our own campus right now. A public, searchable bibliography with a focus on all things digital that uses Zotero, free software for collecting, organizing, annotating, citing, and sharing research. Anyone can view the CDL’s public Zotero library; members of the CDL Zotero group can contribute to it directly. We welcome suggestions for improvement to these resources. We especially welcome direct contributions to those resources built to encourage community participation.

3.title: SUNY Geneseo Center for Digital Learning
3.content: We empower students, faculty, and staff to take control of their digital lives through workshops, resources, events, and project support. </div> Create We can help you build a website using SUNY Create, Geneseo OpenLab, or static site frameworks like Jekyll. Learn more SUNY Create Geneseo OpenLab Jekyll Collaborate We host events, like Geneseo's yearly Douglass Day celebration, that give community members an opportunity to use their digital skills to contribute to the public good. Learn more Douglass Day Ada Lovelace Day Explore We create resources that you can use yourself or share with others to promote thoughtful and effective use of digital technology in service of Geneseo's core values. Learn more Critical Digital Practices CDL Public Zotero Library GenAI: AI at Geneseo Life in Plain Text Why we’re here In a world where all of us are increasingly pressured to adopt “agentic” software, it’s never been more important to possess skills that enable us to be our own agents. “Program or be programmed,” declared the media theorist Douglass Rushkoff in a 2010 book of that title. It’s a stark choice, arguably an oversimplified one. You don’t have to be a programmer to hold onto your digital agency. But at the very least, it’s important to understand some basic things about the computer hardware and software that so thoroughly pervades our lives, if only to distinguish the reality about that hardware and software from the hype. That’s the premise of the CDL’s self-paced course on Critical Digital Practices. (If you do want to learn a little programming, the course will help you with that, too.) Our agency increases when we not only understand digital technology but know how to build with it: to create websites, for example, over which we’re able to exercise creative control — websites that live not on corporate platforms but on hosting we’re able to manage, websites built with open-source tools we’re free to inspect and modify. That’s the premise of our participation in the SUNY-wide initiative SUNY Create, which gives users on participating campuses the ability to manage their own bit of real estate on the web, where they can install open-source software like WordPress or Omeka, or simply host their own files built with Jekyll or another static site generator. Our agency also increases when we have tools that enable us to work effectively with others. That’s the premise of the CDL’s virtual commons, Geneseo OpenLab, built with WordPress and the CUNY Graduate Center’s open-source WordPress plugin Commons In a Box. OpenLab is a social platform where groups can develop projects collaboratively, sharing the fruits of their collaboration on a public-facing website. How we want to work with you With empowerment as our goal, it wouldn’t do for us to build things for you. Come to us with an idea for a research or creative project; it can be your own project or one that you’d like students to engage in. We’ll help you select the tools best suited to it, get you set up, and send you on your way. But you don’t have to make the journey on your own. Call on us for support whenever you need it. We’re happy to help you troubleshoot when you get stuck or continue the conversation about the best path to realizing your vision. Ready to book an appointment? You can do that on the booking site of CDL director Paul Schacht. (Tip: You may want to book two back-to-back, half-hour sessions.) Have an idea for a workshop that would benefit you and fellow faculty, staff, or students? We’d love to run one for you! Pitch your idea in an email to cdl@geneseo.edu.

4.title: Project Guidelines (via Amaranth Studio)
4.content: Project Guidelines (via Amaranth Studio) Tech Stack Static site generator: Jekyll (GitHub Pages compatible) CSS framework: Bootstrap Hosting: GitHub Pages (amaranth-unm.github.io) Related project: Xanthan - the template system Amaranth helps people use Running Locally bundle exec jekyll serve Then visit http://localhost:4000 Project Structure ├── _config.yml # Site configuration ├── _data/ # Data files (YAML) │ ├── events.yml # Events listing │ ├── team.yml # Team member info │ └── top-nav.yml # Navigation structure ├── _includes/ # Reusable components ├── _layouts/ # Page templates (base.html) ├── assets/images/ # All images, organized by type │ ├── headers/ # Page header/hero images (2000px max) │ ├── events/ # Event images (1600px max) │ ├── posters/ # Poster images (1600px max) │ ├── projects/ # Project images (1600px max) │ ├── site/ # General site assets (1600px max) │ └── team/ # Team photos (1200px max) ├── scripts/ # Utility scripts │ ├── README.md # shared with Xanthan — don't edit │ ├── optimize-images.sh # shared with Xanthan — don't edit │ └── update-image-refs.sh # shared with Xanthan — don't edit ├── about/ # "About" menu: studio pages, equipment/, name-origins/ ├── ai/ # "AI" menu ├── public-scholarship/ # "Public Scholarship" menu: websites, posters, audio guides ├── 3d-pedagogy/ # "3D Pedagogy" menu: index is Tactile Learning; printing/, objex/ └── collaborate.md # top-level pages that sit outside the menus Content Guidelines Lead paragraph The first paragraph of body text on every page (immediately after the frontmatter, before any ## heading) must use lead styling and be exactly one paragraph: This is the opening paragraph that sets up the page. {: .lead} Only one paragraph gets {: .lead} — always the first one, never a later one Do not apply {: .lead} to a paragraph that follows a ## heading Keep the lede to 2–4 sentences; it should orient the reader, not summarize the whole page Front Matter Standard page front matter: title: Page Title layout: base date: YYYY-MM-DD header-image: /assets/images/headers/image-name.jpg header-height: 60vh # optional, defaults vary Image Management Adding New Images Place in the correct assets/images/[type]/ folder Use descriptive, hyphenated lowercase names Optimize them — one run per size in the table below (see “Optimizing images”) Verify images display correctly locally Optimizing images The image scripts and the Optimize Images workflow are shared, unmodified, with Xanthan and its sites; scripts/README.md documents them. Don’t edit them here — copy newer versions from xanthan-web. What’s specific to Amaranth is the sizes: No command line: Actions tab → Optimize Images → Run workflow. Set Folder and Longest edge from the table (e.g. assets/images/headers at 2000), run once unticked to preview, then again with Actually change the files ticked. The job limits the longest edge, so a tall image comes out smaller than the width-based commands below would make it; use those for portrait images. Locally: add --preview first to see what would change. bash scripts/optimize-images.sh --no-backup --folder headers --width 2000 bash scripts/optimize-images.sh --no-backup --recursive --base-dir about/name-origins --width 2000 bash scripts/optimize-images.sh --no-backup --folder team --width 1200 # everything else at the default 1600 — name the folders you've added images to bash scripts/optimize-images.sh --no-backup --recursive --base-dir craft --base-dir projects bash scripts/update-image-refs.sh # once at the end, if any PNGs became JPGs Don’t run it with no options or --base-dir . — that would shrink the 2000px images to 1600px. Size Guidelines Type Max Width Use Case headers 2000px Page heroes ScrollStory backgrounds (about/name-origins/images) 2000px Full-screen scrollybox/bg images events/posters/projects/services/site 1600px General content team 1200px Portraits Navigation Navigation is defined in _data/top-nav.yml. Each top-level menu has one folder, and a page lives in the folder of the menu it appears under, so the URL matches the menu (About > Future Directions is about/future-directions.md at /about/future-directions). Pages that aren’t in a menu go in the folder of the section they belong to. When adding new pages: Create the markdown file in the folder for its menu Add entry to top-nav.yml if it should appear in nav Use disabled: true for placeholder/coming-soon items When moving or renaming a page, keep its old URL working: git mv the page together with its images/ folder, update links to it, and add the old URL to its front matter as redirect_from: /old/path (the jekyll-redirect-from plugin builds the redirect). Don’t create top-level folders that share a name with another amaranth-unm repo published under amaranth.unm.edu, such as ai-sketchbook/, reliable-ai/, or campus-history/. Those URLs belong to the separate sites. Common Tasks Adding a new Create folder/page-name.md with proper front matter Add to _data/top-nav.yml if needed Add header image to assets/images/headers/ if using one Adding team members Edit _data/team.yml and add photo to assets/images/team/ Adding events Edit _data/events.yml and add image to assets/images/events/

5.title: Header System Reference (via Amaranth Studio)
5.content: Header System Reference (via Amaranth Studio) NB: Some instructions may not apply to Geneseo installation. All pages with a header-image in front matter are automatically routed through _includes/header-studio.html. There is no separate header-style parameter — every page uses the same system. Front Matter Parameters header-image: /assets/images/headers/my-image.jpg # required — triggers header header-title: My Page Title # shown in header header-tier: section # hero | section | banner (default: hero) header-filter: woodcut # botanical | woodcut | etching | photo (default: photo) header-height: 50vh # overrides CSS default (optional) header-position: "left center" # CSS background-position (default: center right) header-opacity: 0.35 # overrides default opacity for the bg image (optional) Hero-only parameters header-eyebrow: small label above title # Space Mono, all caps, cherry red header-divider: text between decorative lines # sits between two horizontal rules header-subtitle: paragraph below title # light weight, muted Tiers Three tiers control height and typographic scale. Heights are set in CSS (not Liquid) and only overridden when header-height is explicitly set. Tier Default height Background opacity h1 size Use for hero 100vh 0.28 clamp(4–6.5rem) Homepage section 60vh 0.18 clamp(2.2–3.5rem) Section indexes banner 22vh 0.10 clamp(1.3–1.8rem) Interior pages Banner tier uses Space Grotesk (not IM Fell English) for h1 — smaller, more utilitarian. Filters botanical For line-art engravings with dark lines on a white or near-white background — botanical illustrations, fine hatching, pen drawings, woodblock prints on bright white paper. Effect pipeline: invert(1) → dark lines become light → sepia + hue-rotate(320deg) + saturate tints them red → mix-blend-mode: screen makes the (now black/dark) background transparent, so only the glowing red lines show. Requires: The image must have dark marks on a light background. On a dark-background image, invert will flip it wrong. .header-studio-bg--botanical { filter: invert(1) sepia(0.6) hue-rotate(320deg) saturate(2.5); mix-blend-mode: screen; } Tuning: saturate — higher = more vivid red tint (try 2–4) sepia — higher = warmer/more orange; lower = cooler hue-rotate — 310–330deg = red; push toward 340+ for magenta Opacity is not set here — the screen blend mode controls apparent brightness through the image itself. woodcut For early modern prints, woodblock prints, engravings on cream or off-white paper where you want to preserve the tonal warmth of the paper rather than inverting it. Effect pipeline: grayscale(1) neutralizes any color → sepia + hue-rotate + saturate applies red tint → sits on dark background at reduced opacity via mix-blend-mode: normal. No inversion — the woodcut reads as a darkened, reddish version of itself. .header-studio-bg--woodcut { filter: grayscale(1) sepia(1) hue-rotate(320deg) saturate(3) brightness(0.7); mix-blend-mode: normal; opacity: 0.5; /* hero */ } .header-studio--section .header-studio-bg--woodcut { opacity: 0.4; } .header-studio--banner .header-studio-bg--woodcut { opacity: 0.25; } Tuning: brightness(0.7) — controls overall darkness before opacity; lower = darker image opacity — controls how much the dark background shows through; lower = more background, image recedes hue-rotate — 310–330 = red; pushing lower (300–310) adds more magenta saturate — higher = deeper red cast Why not botanical here? Cream paper doesn’t invert cleanly — it becomes a dim blue-grey haze rather than transparent. The contrast(3) pre-boost in the original woodcut version was meant to push cream → white before inverting; the current approach sidesteps this entirely by not inverting. etching For color photos that you want to read as a bold graphic silhouette rather than a photograph. Produces hard-edged black-and-white shapes (stencil aesthetic), not fine lines. Different visual register from botanical/woodcut. Effect pipeline: grayscale → pre-brighten → contrast(5) acts as a threshold, collapsing continuous tone into hard black/white → post-darken → invert → sepia + hue-rotate → saturate tints red → mix-blend-mode: screen makes dark areas transparent. .header-studio-bg--etching { filter: grayscale(1) brightness(1.3) contrast(5) brightness(0.55) invert(1) sepia(0.5) hue-rotate(320deg) saturate(3); mix-blend-mode: screen; } .header-studio--section .header-studio-bg--etching { opacity: 0.40; } .header-studio--banner .header-studio-bg--etching { opacity: 0.25; } Tuning: brightness(1.3) (pre-contrast) — raise to reveal more detail above the threshold; lower to push more areas to black contrast(5) — the threshold step; increase (6–8) for harder edges, decrease (3–4) for softer brightness(0.55) (post-contrast) — controls darkness of the inverted result Note: If you want a photo to produce fine lines (not bold shapes), etching won’t do it. Instead, pre-process the image in Photoshop/GIMP (threshold + edge-detection, or run through an AI line-art tool) and then use botanical. photo For color photos kept photographic — slightly darkened and desaturated. No inversion, no tinting. Use when the image content itself is what matters (a specific place, a specific person, a colorful historical print). .header-studio-bg--photo { filter: saturate(0.9) brightness(0.75); mix-blend-mode: normal; opacity: 0.75; /* hero */ } .header-studio--section .header-studio-bg--photo { opacity: 0.60; } .header-studio--banner .header-studio-bg--photo { opacity: 0.40; } Tuning: opacity — primary control; raise if image looks too faint, lower if text becomes hard to read brightness — secondary; 0.75 is a good baseline for most photos saturate — 0.9 is a subtle desaturation; drop to 0.7 for a more muted look, raise to 1.0 for full color Note on using colorful historical prints: Full-color images (Japanese woodblock prints, illuminated manuscripts, etc.) introduce palettes that don’t exist elsewhere in the design. Use sparingly and intentionally — one or two pages where warmth and color are narratively appropriate. Not as a default. Structural Components These are always present regardless of filter and can be tuned in CSS: Class What it does Key CSS .header-studio-bg The background image div opacity, background-position .header-studio-grid Subtle white grid overlay opacity: 0.025 (hero), lower at smaller tiers .header-studio-bar 4px cherry vertical bar at left edge background: var(--unm-cherry), width .header-studio-content Title text container border-left: 2px solid rgba(186,12,47,0.4), padding, margin-left ::after pseudo-element Gradient fade at bottom height: 350px (hero), less at smaller tiers; fades to #2a2d31 Common Tweaks Image too faint: Increase opacity on .header-studio-bg--[filter] for the relevant tier, or increase brightness in the filter. Image too dominant (text hard to read): Decrease opacity, or decrease brightness. Image focal point in wrong place: Set header-position: "left center" (or any CSS background-position value) in front matter. Section header too tall/short: Set header-height: 45vh (or any vh/px value) in front matter. This applies inline and overrides the CSS default. Opacity for one specific page only: Set header-opacity: 0.25 in front matter — this applies inline to the bg div, overriding the CSS default for that page only. Where Things Live File Role _includes/header-studio.html Liquid template — reads front matter, outputs HTML _layouts/base.html Routes any page with header-image to the studio include assets/css/amaranth-unm.css All header CSS — tiers (~line 979), filters (~line 1164)
